## Solution

### What the demonstrations show

Every output is a 2×2 block. In each pair it is copied unchanged from the top two rows of the input. The only thing that changes is which corner it comes from:

| pair | input size | crop position (y, x) | corner |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 4×4 | (0, 2) | top-right |
| 2 | 3×3 | (0, 0) | top-left |
| 3 | 5×5 | (0, 0) | top-left |

Checking the cells against the grids:
- Pair 1: rows 0–1, columns 2–3 are `8 2 / 4 7`, which is the output.
- Pair 2: the top-left 2×2 is `0 7 / 5 6`, which is the output.
- Pair 3: the top-left 2×2 is `5 8 / 8 0`, which is the output.

The colours in the copied cells vary between pairs and do not mark the chosen spot. The fact sheet also lists no other feature, such as a marker or a repeated object, that singles out the corner. The parity of the side length does separate the cases cleanly:
- The 4×4 grid has an even side and gives the top-right corner.
- The 3×3 and 5×5 grids have odd sides and give the top-left corner.

The supplied reference program uses exactly this rule.

There is a limitation. Only one even example exists, so the even-side half of the rule rests on a single pair. Still, it is the simplest rule consistent with all three demonstrations.

### Applying it to the test

The test grid is 8×8. Its side is even, so we crop rows 0–1 and columns 6–7:



### Construction stages
The work is a single crop, so there is one emit, of the final 2×2 canvas.
code:
def transform(grid):
    g = np.array(grid)
    h, w = g.shape
    # Even side -> top-right 2x2 corner; odd side -> top-left 2x2 corner.
    x = w - 2 if w % 2 == 0 else 0
    out = g[:2, x:x + 2].copy()
    side = "even" if w % 2 == 0 else "odd"
    corner = "top-right" if w % 2 == 0 else "top-left"
    emit(out, f"Grid side {w} is {side}, so copy the {corner} 2x2 block (rows 0-1, columns {x}-{x+1}).")
    return out
